part.title: Planning a presentation on city noise

turns.text: So, Marcus, we really need to lock in the plan for our presentation today. It's due in three weeks, and we haven't even agreed on sources.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I know. First, though, I feel like we should explain to Professor Novak why we didn't take her suggestion. She proposed light pollution, remember?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. I don't think she'll mind, though. And it's not as if we turned it down because there wasn't enough material. There's loads on light pollution.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: True. Honestly, it was the construction outside my apartment that settled it. They've been drilling for the new light rail line since September, and I haven't slept past seven in weeks.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I remember you complaining. Okay, sources. I think the World Health Organization guidelines on environmental noise have to be at the center of everything.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Isn't that report kind of old, though? I think it came out in 2018.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: It's a few years old, sure, but almost every study I've found refers back to it. So it's really the obvious place to start.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. Some of the appendices are pretty technical, though.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: We don't need those. Just the main recommendations, like the safe levels for nighttime noise.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Okay. What about that newspaper article I sent you, the one about Toronto?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I read it. At first I wondered if it was paid for by that soundproof window company, because their ad was right next to it. But no, it's a genuine piece of journalism.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So we can use it?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I'd rather not. It's full of figures, like how many people are exposed to heavy traffic noise, but it never says where any of them come from. We can't cite numbers like that.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Hmm, shame. And I didn't think the fact that it's about a Canadian city was a problem at all.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No, that part was fine. So, what about our own measurements? Did you get the sound meter from the department?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yes, I picked it up yesterday. I was planning to stand by the interstate, but I checked, and there's nowhere safe to stand that's close enough to the traffic.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: And campus is too quiet to show anything interesting, apart from the dining hall at lunchtime, maybe.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So why don't we take the readings right where the light rail work is happening, on University Avenue? We could measure once during the drilling and once after the crews go home.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Perfect. That gives us a nice contrast. Now, how should we split up the work?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Well, I'm happy to make all the slides if you do most of the talking. I'm much better at design than at public speaking.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Professor Novak said she wants to hear from both of us equally, though. So I think we just divide it down the middle. I'll research and present the first three sections, and you take the last three.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Okay, that's fair. And we can each make our own slides, as long as we agree on a template.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sounds good. When should we meet next? I can't do Thursday, I've got a lab all afternoon.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: How about Saturday? Oh, sorry, no, I'm working Saturday. Sunday afternoon?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sunday afternoon works. Second floor of the library, around two?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure, see you there.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Oh, before you go, let me run through what Professor Novak said about each section when I met her on Monday. I took notes.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great, because I missed that meeting.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: So, for the introduction, she said not to start with definitions. She wants us to get the audience involved right away, for example by asking them how many were woken up by noise this week.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Oh. I'd thought we could open with a recording of rush-hour traffic.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: She liked the recording idea, but she thought it fits better when we talk about where city noise comes from. So in the main sources section, we'll play a short clip of the drilling instead.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Nice. And health effects?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: She was quite strict about that one. There are lots of blogs out there that exaggerate the risks, so she wants us to stick to studies published in proper academic journals.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Makes sense. Then the case study, which is mine. I was thinking of comparing Minneapolis with Toronto.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: She actually warned against that. She said two cities would be far too much for a ten-minute talk. Stay with Minneapolis, but show where the noisiest neighborhoods are on a map of the city.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Okay. What did she say about solutions?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That students always list great ideas, like quieter road surfaces or noise barriers, but forget to say what they'd cost. So she wants at least a rough estimate of the price of each one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And the conclusion? Anything special for that part?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: She didn't care whether we include statistics there or not, which honestly surprised me a bit. Her only point was that it should be brief, two minutes at most.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Got it. Right, I'll start working on the map tonight.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.heard: So, Marcus, we really need to lock in the plan for our presentation today. It's due in three weeks, and we haven't even agreed on sources.
Yeah, I know. First, though, I feel like we should explain to Professor Novak why we didn't take her suggestion. She proposed light pollution, remember?
Right, I don't think she'll mind though, and it's not as if we turned it down because there wasn't enough material. There's loads on light pollution.
True, honestly, it was the construction outside my apartment that settled it; they've been drilling for the new light rail line since September and I haven't slept past seven in weeks.
I remember you complaining. Okay, sources. I think the World Health Organization guidelines on environmental noise have to be at the center of everything.
Isn't that report kinda old, though? I think it came out in 2018.
It's a few years old, sure, but almost every study I've found refers back to it, so it's really the obvious place to start.
Fair enough. Some of the appendices are pretty technical though.
We don't need those, just the main recommendations, like the safe levels for nighttime noise.
Okay, what about that newspaper article I sent you, the one about Toronto?
I read it. At first I wondered if it was paid for by that soundproof window company, because their ad was right next to it. But no, it's a genuine piece of journalism.
So we can use it?
I'd rather not. It's full of figures, like how many people are exposed to heavy traffic noise, but it never says where any of them come from. We can't cite numbers like that.
Hmm, shame, and I didn't think the fact that it's about a Canadian city was a problem at all.
No, that part was fine. So, what about our own measurements? Did you get the sound meter from the department?
Yes, I picked it up yesterday. I was planning to stand by the interstate, but I checked, and there's nowhere safe to stand that's close enough to the traffic.
And campus is too quiet to show anything interesting, apart from the dining hall at lunchtime maybe.
So why don't we take the readings right where the light rail work is happening, on University Avenue? We could measure once during the drilling and once after the crews go home.
Perfect, that gives us a nice contrast. Now, how should we split up the work?
Well, I'm happy to make all the slides if you do most of the talking. I'm much better at design than at public speaking.
Professor Novak said she wants to hear from both of us equally though, so I think we just divide it down the middle. I'll research and present the first three sections and you take the last three.
Okay, that's fair, and we can each make our own slides as long as we agree on a template.
Sounds good. When should we meet next? I can't do Thursday, I've got a lab all afternoon.
How about Saturday? Oh, sorry, no, I'm working Saturday. Sunday afternoon?
Sunday afternoon works. Second floor of the library, around two?
Sure, see you there!
Oh, before you go, let me run through what Professor Novak said about each section when I met her on Monday. I took notes.
Great, because I missed that meeting.
So, for the introduction, she said not to start with definitions. She wants us to get the audience involved right away, for example by asking them how many were woken up by noise this week.
Oh, I'd thought we could open with a recording of rush hour traffic.
She liked the recording idea, but she thought it fits better when we talk about where city noise comes from, so in the main sources section we'll play a short clip of the drilling instead.
Nice. And health effects?
She was quite strict about that one. There are lots of blogs out there that exaggerate the risks, so she wants us to stick to studies published in proper academic journals.
Makes sense. Then the case study, which is mine, I was thinking of comparing Minneapolis with Toronto.
She actually warned against that. She said two cities would be far too much for a ten-minute talk. Stay with Minneapolis, but show where the noisiest neighborhoods are on a map of the city.
Okay, what did she say about solutions?
That students always list great ideas, like quieter road surfaces or noise barriers, but forget to say what they'd cost, so she wants at least a rough estimate of the price of each one.
And the conclusion? Anything special for that part?
She didn't care whether we include statistics there or not, which honestly surprised me a bit. Her only point was that it should be brief, two minutes at most.
Got it. Right, I'll start working on the map tonight.
